item.title: India's WTC Final chances: What South Africa's win over Australia means
item.description: South Africa's innings-and-31-run victory over Australia in the second Test in Gqeberha has made the race for the World Test Championship (WTC) final more competitive. Although Australia remain at the top of the standings, the defeat stops them from extending their lead and gives other teams, including India, some hope. Australia have a points percentage (PCT) of 75.00, while New Zealand are second at 72.22 and South Africa sit third at 66.67. — ICC (@ICC) What India need to do India are currently fifth in the standings, with seven Tests remaining in the cycle — two against New Zealand and five against Australia at home. To finish with a PCT of 60, India need to collect 62 points from these matches and cannot afford to lose more than two Tests. However, even a strong finish may not guarantee qualification. India also need at least two of Australia, New Zealand and South Africa to drop points in their remaining matches. Their upcoming series against New Zealand and Australia will therefore be crucial to their chances of reaching the final at The Oval in London next year. 135139540 Bangladesh also in the race Bangladesh, currently fourth, remain in contention for a place in the final. Four of their six remaining Tests will be played at home, giving them an opportunity to collect valuable points. They will need to make the most of home conditions and hope that teams above them lose points. South Africa's win has kept the competition open, but India still face a difficult task and will need both consistent performances and favourable results elsewhere to reach the final.

item.title: Tchouameni reveals truth behind reported Real Madrid bust-up with Valverde
item.description: Tchouameni reveals truth behind reported Real Madrid bust-up with Valverde Although the team has been struggling on the pitch for quite some time, Real Madrid had a particularly calamitous last season, when their problems transcended the pitch and penetrated into the dressing room as well. There were several indications of this phenomenon, but the most prominent of these came late in the season, as news emerged of a dressing room fight between two important players , Federico Valverde and Aurelien Tchouameni. However, this episode already seems to be a thing of the past. The two players have already played and celebrated their team’s success on the pitch together this season. In fact, as Diario AS has reported, one of these players, Tchouameni, appeared in an interview with The Bridge and outright denied that there was a physical altercation between him and the Uruguayan: “People talk a lot, but there was no fight between Valverde and me. Yes, it’s true that things happen in the dressing room, but we never fought. In a dressing room, there are indirect remarks and things like that, but I never got into a fight with Valverde. It’s true that something unpleasant happened. The only problem with all this is that it’s Real Madrid, and anything, no matter how small, gets blown out of proportion and becomes a massive media circus. Something that wasn’t necessarily a problem ends up becoming one.” The Real Madrid midfielder believed that such disputes were common in any dressing room: “Afterwards, everyone called me to ask what had happened and whether I was all right. They want to know what happened, but these days you have to be very discreet. To reassure people, I had to tell them that nothing was wrong. I once watched an NFL documentary, and these things happen very often there.” For now, Tchouameni assured that there are no problems between him and Valverde, and went on to indicate that their relationship might even be better than before: “If you walk into the dressing room today, as Mourinho said, you’ll see that Valverde and I are fine. There’s no problem between us. There’s no problem on the pitch either; life goes on. In fact, these kinds of things can bring you even closer to the other person. We’re fine, and we have no problems with each other.” The signs that the two players have gotten over their differences were already there, but these statements from Aurelien Tchouameni only go on to confirm this. Hopefully, Jose Mourinho will be able to keep the dressing room environment healthy and eliminate all the other problems that plagued that team last season.

item.title: Jones: ‘100% Inter can win the Champions League, the gap isn’t that far away’
item.description: Jones: ‘100% Inter can win the Champions League, the gap isn’t that far away’ Curtis Jones has no doubts that Inter have what it takes to challenge on all fronts this season, and insists that the ‘gap isn’t that far away’ between the Nerazzurri and the Champions League trophy: ‘I just feel that the team has what it takes’. The former Liverpool midfielder spoke in-depth about his journey with Inter thus far in an interview with DAZN, which was released on Friday. Jones on start to life in Italy, his best characteristics and Inter’s Champions League hopes Inter sit at the top of the Serie A standings after seven matches: Jones has earned one start in the league so far, missing the last two with an adductor injury. He has made it clear that scoring his first Nerazzurri goal is the first thing he wants to tick off upon his return to action. MILAN, ITALY – SEPTEMBER 14: Ange-Yoan Bonny of FC Internazionale Milano celebrates scoring his team’s fifth goal with teammate Curtis Jones during the Serie A match between FC Internazionale and Udinese Calcio at Stadio Giuseppe Meazza on September 14, 2026 in Milan, Italy. (Photo by Claudio Villa/Getty Images) “I just want to score, whether it’s like that or a tap-in [after being shown a clip of his first goal for Liverpool against Everton, a screamer from outside the penalty area]. “A goal’s a goal and I just want to help the team. I want to show the fans that I can help the team challenge for the Champions League, win the league again.” Jones’s former Liverpool teammate Alexander Isak described him as the most underrated player he has played alongside. In response, Jones said: “It’s nice, yes. It’s a compliment as well. It’s not only him who’s said that it’s been said by lads in the past that I’ve played with, so it’s good that there are teammates of mine who appreciate me. item.title: Andre Onana: Man United goalkeeper caught up in terrifying incident hours after playing
item.description: Andre Onana: Man United goalkeeper caught up in terrifying incident hours after playing Manchester United’s on-loan keeper Andre Onana has been involved in a serious car crash in Turkey but is thankfully ok. Season Onana struggled massively during his two seasons at Old Trafford and was a pillar of inconsistency. As a result, he was moved out on loan to Trabzonspor in Turkey and continued for a second season this year. The Cameroonian keeper has impressed for the most part, keeping four clean sheets in five matches lately. Nonetheless, he has still had the odd blunder in him as he conceded directly from a corner last week in the Conference League. Incident Onana was coming back from the match last night, which his side won 2-0 against Scottish side Heart of Midlothian. The Sun newspaper reports that, “Andre Onana has cheated death in a terrifying road accident – with the Manchester United keeper’s car involved in a multi-vehicle pile-up.” The report continues that the keeper and “his family were then caught up in a frightening drama as he drove home after the game.” The paper describes the incident as “another vehicle reportedly crashed into the 30-year-old’s car from behind at high speed – shunting the luxurious silver vehicle into the back of the car in front of him.” Emergency services raced to the scene on the Yomra road close to the Black Sea, and the keeper was taken to hospital. Fortunately, he was discharged after medical checks. Trabzonspor president Ertugrul Dogan released a statement commenting, “Andre Onana was involved in a road traffic accident earlier this evening. There are no problems with him, and we wish him a speedy recovery.” It remains to be seen whether he will be in condition to play in Trabzonspor’s next match on Monday evening against Çaykur Rizespor. item.title: Erling Haaland '100% available' as Man City take on Aston Villa
item.description: FILE PHOTO - Manchester City's Erling Haaland celebrates scoring their side's third goal of the game during the English Premier League match between Manchester City and Ipswich Town at the Etihad Stadium. (is associated with: «Erling Haaland '100% available' as Man City take on Aston Villa») Martin Rickett/PA Wire/dpa Top scorer Erling Haaland is set to return as Manchester City travel to Aston Villa this weekend. The prolific Norway striker was not risked in City's Champions League victory over AEK Athens in midweek after a blow to the foot in the previous game against Ipswich. Haaland scored twice against the Tractor Boys last Saturday, taking his goal tally for the season to 12, but limped off at full-time and was an unused substitute on Tuesday. City will continue to assess Nico O'Reilly, Mateo Kovacic and Matheus Nunes, who also suffered knocks in the same game. Manager Enzo Maresca said: "They could all be available or not. There are still doubts. "Erling is the only one who is 100% available and for the other three we need to wait." City have started the season superbly, with Maresca becoming the first manager to win his first seven Premier League games after taking charge of a new club. They are three points clear at the top of the table ahead of Saturday's trip to Villa Park. Their only defeats this term have come against champions Arsenal in the Community Shield and Europe's top side Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League. Their form has also shown no signs of being affected by the storm that has surrounded the club since last month's guilty verdict for breaching financial regulations. "The mood is very good," said Maresca. "We are happy with our start but we are hungry for more wins." The goals have also been flowing, with 23 scored in the last six games, but Maresca feels there is still room for improvement. "We need to find the right balance between the goals we score and the goals we concede," the Italian said. "In this moment we are scoring many goals but I'm sure that we can improve. There is always something that we can do better. This is our target." Villa made a slow start to the campaign after losing key players in the summer but are now unbeaten in six games and have also impressed in Europe. Maresca said: "I have huge respect for Unai Emery. He's a fantastic manager and they are a very good team. "You can see clearly what they want, they are very intense off the ball and in this moment they are in a good mood, they are winning games. I am sure, 100 per cent, it is going to be a tough game."

There's no longer any incentive for those universities to schedule nonconference games against quality opponents. In the Southeastern Conference and Big Ten, just get through the season with three losses or fewer and you can punch your ticket. In fact, if you're Notre Dame, a school that everyone wants to play and sets its own schedule, you're the master of your own fate. Play it coy, eliminate the USCs, BYUs and, of course, Michigan and you're guaranteed a berth in the future format. item.title: There's a new playoff format for (some) Colorado high school football
item.description: As the 2026 Colorado high school football regular season winds down, it's a good reminder that there are some playoff format changes for this two-year CHSAA cycle. Classes 3A and 2A now have expanded playoffs to match 4A and 5A. The old 16-team brackets are out, with the 2A and 3A postseason fields now including 24 teams. Like the upper classes, that means the top eight seeds in those classifications receive first-round byes, hosting the winners of first-round games between seeds Nos. 9-24. Playoff expansion impacts in Class 3A football The Colorado Class 3A schedule and format is now identical to the 4A and 5A classifications. Previously, the 3A regular season ended a week later to align its early-December championship dates with the upper classes, due to having the smaller 16-team bracket. The expanded 3A field is already having a noticeable impact this season. Take some Northern Colorado teams, for example. NoCo teams like Berthoud (No. 13), Windsor (No. 16) and Silver Creek (No. 18) would be fighting for their playoff lives under the old 16-team format. While another win in the final two weeks would still be beneficial, these teams are likely safe to make the 24-team field. Colorado Class 2A playoff impacts, host differences Class 2A now finishes its regular season one week earlier to accommodate the extra week needed for an expanded 24-team field, while still playing its championship on the last weekend of November with Class 1A and 8/6-man football. Despite the 2A bracket and format being the same as the upper classifications, there are different hosting rules for 2A playoff games. In Classes 3A through 5A, the higher seed hosts every playoff game until the state championship. In Colorado Class 2A, the higher seed still hosts its first game. However, the home team for quarterfinal matchups "shall be that team which has had the fewer home games during the state playoffs. If both teams have had an equal number of home games the team with the higher designation will host that game." The higher seed in 2A is still guaranteed to host in the semifinal round. Host sites, schedule for CHSAA football state championship games 6/8-man and 1A/2A state title games: Nov. 27 (1:30 p.m.): 6-man state championship Nov. 27 (5 p.m.): 8-man state championship Nov. 28 (1:30 p.m.): 1A state championship Nov. 28 (5 p.m.): 2A state championship (Games at CSU-Pueblo ThunderBowl) 3A/4A/5A state title games: Dec. 5 (10 a.m.): 3A state championship Dec. 5 (1:30 p.m.) 4A state championship Dec. 5 (5 p.m.): 5A state championship (Games at CSU's Canvas Stadium) Chris Abshire covers high school and community sports for the Coloradoan. Houston Rockets forward Kevin Durant ($104.9 million), Miami Heat forward Giannis Antetokounmpo ($103.5 million) and Minnesota Timberwolves guard Anthony Edwards ($87.9 million) round out the top five. That ascending contract structure has major pitfalls, though, particularly in the NBA’s second-apron era. Teams are becoming more wary of handing out big-money, long-term contracts, especially to older players. One wrong step can lead to an albatross contract that effectively ruins a team’s chances of contending for a championship. LeBron made the unprecedented decision this summer to go from a $52.6 million max contract to a $3.9 million veteran-minimum deal, but he isn’t the only older star who’s taken a below-max contract in recent years. Curry signed a two-year, $116 million extension in September that was roughly $20 million less than he could have earned. That trend has caught the eye of the National Basketball Players Association, which is setting the stage for the NBA’s next major labor battle . “We think the players should make decisions for themselves and we should not be ... pocket-watching,” NBPA executive president David Kelly told reporters in July. “The system should not require a player to carry all of that burden. We should not put a player in the position to carry the burden of keeping a team together.” The NBA’s current collective bargaining agreement runs through 2029-30, but either side can opt out after the 2028-29 season. Given the NBPA’s saber-rattling about the second apron, this CBA likely has only three years left, which means both sides should already be preparing for another round of labor negotiations. If the second apron remains in place, Forbes’ list of highest-paid players could help provide a solution to the NBA’s current dilemma with its contract structure. Reimagining NBA Contracts Remove off-court earnings momentarily and just look at the league’s highest-paid players in terms of their 2026-27 cap hit. Among the top 12, Jayson Tatum is the only one who won’t be at least 30 years old by the end of October. (Jaylen Brown turns 30 on Oct. 24, while Devin Booker turns 30 six days later.) The Boston Celtics openly admitted that they traded Brown this offseason in large part for financial reasons. Team president Brad Stevens told reporters the Celtics’ path back toward title contention “looked a little bit more challenging with 70% of our cap and such a high percentage of our usage tied into two players [Brown and Tatum].” The Sixers traded Paul George, whom they signed to a four-year, $211.6 million max contract two summers ago, to acquire Brown. George played only 78 games during his two seasons in Philly due to a combination of injuries and a 25-game suspension for violating the NBA’s anti-drug policy. His contract became an albatross almost as soon as the ink dried on it. That’s a byproduct of the NBA’s current contract rules, which divvy up percentages of the salary cap based on years of experience in the league. The problem is that teams often wind up paying players more once they’re past their prime than they did in the midst of it. The NBA’s dilemma harkens back to the infamous comments that Toronto Blue Jays first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. made earlier this year. “I want people to understand one thing. The money they gave me wasn’t for what I’m going to do. It was for what I already did,” Guerrero said in an interview . “They didn’t pay me because I’m going to hit 40 [home runs] every year. They paid me for what I already accomplished.” In essence, the NBA’s system forces teams to do the same. They’re able to pay players a greater percentage of the salary cap when they’re in their mid-30s than they can in their mid-20s. That’s counterintuitive in terms of expected production moving forward. But what if endorsements could help bridge the gap? A Potential Solution? Outside of Curry, LeBron, Durant and Giannis, most of the league’s highest-paid players derive a majority of their earnings from their NBA salary. Edwards, Tatum and two-time reigning MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander are all earning an estimated $25 million or more from endorsements this year, but Warriors forward Jimmy Butler (No. 7 overall), Phoenix Suns guard Devin Booker (No. 9 overall) and Sixers center Joel Embiid (No. 10 overall) are each pulling in less than an estimated $15 million in off-court earnings. Still, it stands to reason that the more established an NBA star is, the more likely he is to sign lucrative endorsement deals. And since their off-court earnings typically only rise further into their careers, that could help offset any declines in their on-court earnings once they reach their mid-30s. That begs the question: Should the NBA rethink its contract system to give teams the ability to pay players the most when they’re at their peak? Could endorsements and investments help stars make up the difference later in their careers even if they can’t earn as much from their NBA contracts? The easiest solution would be to allow teams to give 35% max deals to players with 7-9 years of experience and then begin dialing back how much players can earn after that, particularly once they reach their mid-30s. However, that isn’t as simple as it might sound. Under current NBA rules, a player’s max salary is never lower than 105% of his previous salary, so the new rules would have to account for how to handle players who receive a 35% max earlier in their careers. Another oft-proposed solution is allowing teams to still hand out 35% max contracts to older stars, but only having 30% of that count against a team’s cap sheet. Granted, that would run counter to the NBA’s push for “parity of opportunity,” which includes redistributing star talent around the league in part for financial reasons. Maintaining the status quo could be another option. Teams are allowed to introduce players to potential sponsors, although they need to be particularly careful about following the NBA’s rules after the Los Angeles Clippers’ salary-cap circumvention scandal. Making the introduction is the extent of their allowable involvement; anything beyond that could get them into stripped-first-round-pick territory. Either way, Curry and the Warriors will be instructive over the next year. item.title: The player Butch Harmon called the future of the PGA Tour who only won three times in his career
item.description: Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images Even at the peak of Tiger Woods’ powers, the golfing world was searching for his heir. Woods dominated the sport like no one we have ever seen, taking golf to a new stratosphere of global popularity. But significant concerns remain about what happens when the greatest golfer of all time is no longer around. The PGA Tour wrestled with this for the better part of a decade, until Rory McIlroy and Bryson DeChambeau’s feud relit a spark in the sport’s popularity. But back in 2008, Woods’ former coach, Butch Harmon, thought he’d found golf’s next superstar. Butch Harmon said Anthony Kim was the ‘future of golf’ It looked like Anthony Kim would take the golfing world by storm back in 2008. In his second year as a pro, he won twice on the PGA Tour at just 23. Kim’s early career was so impressive that he convinced Harmon he was the future of the PGA Tour. He told the Guardian in 2008, “This kid is the future of golf on the PGA Tour. I like his golf game, I like his confidence, and I like the fact that he has come out on tour and contended straight away, just like he said he would. It ain’t bragging if you can back it up.” Harmon wasn’t the only one who bought into Kim’s talent. One of Woods’ old friends and rivals, Mark O’Meara, said that Woods is the only player he’s ever seen that was more talented than Kim. He even went as far as to say that Kim’s swing was better than Woods. He said, “I see a lot of talented young players. Nothing really jumped out at me until I played with this kid. I was like, whoa, this guy has got some game because he plays the little shots. “He wants to win. He has got as much talent as, or more than, any other player I’ve ever seen besides Tiger. At 22 I think Tiger’s mental game was probably stronger. Technique-wise, swing-wise, I reckon his swing is better at 21, 22 than what Tiger’s was.” Kim was projected for greatness, but unfortunately his story became something of a “what if?” After peaking at No. 6 in the Official World Golf Ranking, Kim’s career derailed due to a severe string of injuries. He suffered an Achilles tendon injury in 2012, alongside multiple surgeries on his shoulder, hand, and spine. Kim’s struggles with drug and alcohol addiction also played a deeply destructive role in both his initial downfall and his 12-year absence from the sport. While physical injuries initially forced him off the PGA Tour in 2012, his substance abuse heavily compounded his problems behind the scenes. Kim is now 41, with three PGA Tour wins and an incredible comeback victory on LIV Golf this year. He’s now got his life back together, but his career promised so much more. item.title: Costly Drake Maye mistake looms large in Patriots’ loss to Bears
item.description: Standing at the postgame podium, Drake Maye shook his head and looked down at ground. He let out an audible sigh of frustration. The Patriots quarterback was replaying his second-quarter interception that helped swing Thursday night’s loss to the Chicago Bears . “Huge point in the game. Gosh,” Maye said after the game. “Those plays can swing the game, can impact the game, and that was definitely one of them right there. I wish I definitely had that one back.” After a slow offensive start Thursday night while dealing with Chicago’s pressure packages, New England’s offense found its footing with a pair of strong drives to open the second quarter. Maye finished the first with a rushing touchdown, then led the Patriots back into the red zone with a chance to take the lead. Instead, his pass up the seam to rookie tight end Eli Raridon sailed short and was intercepted. “We hit the same thing, the same exact play later in the game,” Maye said, recalling his 30-yard touchdown pass to Raridon in third quarter quarter. “I like my chances in there. It’s frustrating … I let my team down.” The interception cost the Patriots a chance to add seven points, a missed opportunity that loomed large in their 30-24 to the Bears. Trailing 27-21 in the fourth quarter, New England had two possessions to take the lead but managed just one first down between them. The Bears then drained more than 11 minutes of clock across their following two possessions. Those missed opportunities weighed on Maye as much as the interception. “That’s probably what I’ll be thinking about most over the weekend, having two chances with the ball down 27-21,” Maye said. “We got a good chance to go score and trust our defense … We just fell short tonight.” Despite the costly turnover, Maye kept New England within striking distance against Caleb Williams and Chicago’s high-powered offense. With little help from the running game, he completed a season-high 77.4% of his passes and was nearly perfect against pressure, completing 11 of 12 attempts for 151 yards and a touchdown. “He gave us a chance. He competed,” head coach Mike Vrabel said. “I know he’d like to have that one back. He’ll learn from it like he always does. I’m glad he’s ours.”

As both teams seek their first World Series title ever, here is how each owner first made his fortune. Milwaukee Brewers: Mark Attanasio Born in the Bronx, where he grew up rooting for the New York Yankees, Attanasio graduated from Columbia Law School in 1982 and worked at the prestigious firm Debevoise & Plimpton. By his third year, he was having second thoughts about spending the rest of his career climbing the ranks toward partnership. “I didn’t want my whole life planned out at 26,” he later recalled . Patrick McDermott/Getty Images After moving to California to join Drexel Burnham Lambert, the Wall Street investment bank that helped popularize junk bonds, Attanasio initially worked in mergers and acquisitions but became more interested in trading. The company built just 27 homes in 2009, but its business took off as the market recovered. By 2013, Dream Finders had sold more than 1,000 homes. item.title: Edu becomes Northampton advisor after Forest exit
item.description: Former Arsenal and Valencia midfielder Edu won 16 caps for Brazil [Getty Images] Nottingham Forest's former global head of football Edu will serve as a senior advisor to the new owners of Northampton Town, the League Two club has confirmed. The former Arsenal and Brazil midfielder departed his role at the Premier League club in September and has since joined the board of directors at Bulgarian top - flight club Levski Sofia. A Brazilian consortium featuring former AC Milan and Chelsea forward Alexandre Pato last month, completed a takeover of Northampton, who are 23rd in League Two, last month. Speaking at an open forum event, Cobblers co-chairman Joao Xavier said Edu would help the club navigate "sporting questions" on an ad-hoc basis. Levski Sofia are owned by London-based investment firm Gemcorp Capital, who are an investor in Sports Alpha Capital - the group which has become Northampton's majority shareholder. Asked about Edu's role, Xavier said: "We are very proud to have Alex [Pato] with us and Edu with us too. "We became friends as he had a role at Nottingham Forest and I asked him to help me learn more about English football. "Edu is a senior advisor for one of our partners, acting as an advisor for Levski Sofia and also here, helping us navigate the sporting questions here at the club, not day to day, just when we ask him and when we need him. "The club will never be part of a multi-club ownership, no other club is part of our project." Who are Northampton Town's new owners? Edu's position at Forest came under the spotlight after a falling-out with Nuno Espirito Santo, who was sacked last September, the first of four managers at Forest over the 2025-26 campaign. He arrived after six years at Arsenal, where he became the club's first sporting director in 2022, having won two Premier League titles and two FA Cups as a midfielder with the Gunners. He brought Mikel Arteta to Emirates Stadium, who delivered the club's first Premier League title in 22 years last season. item.title: Arsenal women confirmed for new FIFA tournament starting in 2028
item.description: Arsenal women confirmed for new FIFA tournament starting in 2028 The 2028 tournament will bring together 19 clubs from around the world, with Arsenal qualifying through their Champions League success. Photo by Harry Murphy/Getty Images Arsenal will take part in the first FIFA Women’s Club World Cup after being named among the first seven clubs confirmed for the new competition. The tournament will be held in the United States from 5 – 30 January, 2028, and will feature 19 clubs from all six confederations. FIFA confirmed Arsenal’s place on 22 October 2026, with the competition set to be played every four years. Arsenal qualified by winning the Women’s Champions League , with European champions from the seasons ending between 2024 and 2027 earning a place at the tournament. The remaining UEFA spots will be decided by club rankings. Photo by Maja Hitij/Getty Images Alongside Arsenal, Barcelona , Club América , Gotham FC , Corinthians , Naegohyang Women’s FC and Wuhan Jiangda have also qualified. That leaves 12 of the 19 places still to be filled. Europe gets six spots, the biggest allocation of any confederation. Asia , Africa , Concacaf and South America each get three, while Oceania gets one. For UEFA, repeat Women’s Champions League winners will open up extra places through the rankings. Normally, no more than two clubs from the same country can qualify, although there is an exception if more than two clubs from one country win the Champions League during the qualifying period. Photo by Maja Hitij/Getty Images

item.title: Boulter into Japan semis and back as British No 1
item.description: Katie Boulter is through to her third WTA semi-final of the 2026 season [Getty Images] Katie Boulter has reclaimed the British number one ranking after fighting back to beat Antonia Ruzic in three sets in the quarter-finals of the Japan Open. The 30-year-old was dethroned on Monday following Sonay Kartal's run to the final in Wuhan but knew she could overturn the 55-point deficit by reaching the last four in Osaka. Eighth seed Boulter trailed world number 91 Ruzic by a set and a break but recovered to win 3-6 6-3 6-3 in two hours to reach her first semi-final since Queen's in June. She will face Czech Katerina Siniakova in the last four and whatever the result will climb above Kartal and back into the world's top 50 when the WTA rankings are updated on Monday. "[Ruzic] is a really good player, full credit to her," said Boulter. "I tried to hang tough and find a way. I was a bit lucky in the middle of the second [set] but I feel I did really well to stay there." On facing Siniakova for a spot in the final, she added: "She's one hell of a player, extremely dangerous. It's going to be who gets the first strike in. "I've got nothing to lose. She's been building extremely well this week, so I'm going to have to come prepared." Inside British number one Kartal's remarkable comeback Boulter struggled on serve in the opening two sets, winning just 60% points behind her first serve, hitting four double faults, and facing seven break points, but grew into the match, finding success when stepping inside the baseline to put pressure on the 23-year-old Croat. Broken in her opening service game, Boulter was gifted a route back into the first set at 4-2 when Ruzic double-faulted on break point. item.title: Arsenal identify surprise January target from Atletico Madrid to solve winger crisis and it is not who fans expect
item.description: Newcastle United v Atletico Madrid - Pre-Season Friendly - Getty Images Sport Arsenal are plotting a winter transfer raid on Spanish giants Atletico Madrid as Mikel Arteta looks to address a glaring shortage of wide options at the Emirates Stadium. Recruitment chiefs have turned their attention back to versatile La Liga winger Alex Baena after sanctioning two high-profile attacking departures during the summer window. Gunners revive Spanish winger pursuit The north Londoners are preparing a January approach for Atletico attacker Baena as they seek a new left winger for the second half of the campaign. Having offloaded both Gabriel Martinelli and Leandro Trossard over the summer, the Premier League champions only recruited Christos Tzolis as a direct replacement . Capable of operating on either flank or centrally, the 25-year-old fits the profile required by the coaching staff. Prolific form complicates winter negotiations imago-sport-1084841887.jpg According to FootballTransfers , the Spain international has been "identified as a potential January signing" by the Emirates Stadium hierarchy. The outlet adds that the English club previously "targeted Baena in 2024" prior to his move from Villarreal to the Spanish capital and are now "revisiting a potential move" ahead of the mid-season window. However, prising him away from the Metropolitano will prove difficult given his contract runs until 2030 and head coach Diego Simeone regards him as a key figure after he registered five goals and two assists across nine appearances this term. Argentine striker remains parallel objective Baena is not the only Atletico star on the Gunners' radar, with the club also maintaining their interest in his attacking team-mate Julian Alvarez after making the Argentine their primary summer target. While the forward remained in Madrid, his valuation has reportedly dropped from the €150 million (£126.8m / $168.3m) quoted during the close season down to €120m (£101.5m / $134.7m). To help finance a mid-season bid, Arsenal are prepared to cash in on Viktor Gyokeres and have slapped a £64m valuation on the Swedish striker, a fee that would cover over half of the outlay required for the World Cup winner. Striker preference threatens ambitious swoop imago-sport-1084827805.jpg Even if the Gunners raise funds through player sales to meet Atletico's asking price for Alvarez, their pursuit is complicated by the striker's desire to join La Liga rivals Barcelona . Negotiating mid-season deals for either attacking talent will test the resolve of the Spanish outfit when the market reopens in the new year. Consequently, Arsenal face tough talks in Madrid if they are to bolster their frontline in January.

item.title: Chaotic state of football in Brazil epitomises a nation where greed has conquered glory | Jonathan Liew
item.description: The national game merely reflects the mood in a divided nation which is going to the polls with very little faith in the power of democracy Look, cards on the table: I don’t know for certain, and nor do you, whether Flávio Bolsonaro – the man widely tipped to become the next president of Brazil after Sunday night’s election – really did steal an island from Richarlison. There are lawyers involved, claims and counter-claims, and in any case, adjudicating land ownership disputes between right-wing strongmen and Tottenham reserve-team strikers lies very much beyond this column’s spectrum of expertise. It’s why, for example, this newspaper took no official position on the well-publicised battle between Rodrigo Duterte and Vincent Janssen over that Polynesian isthmus. According to Richarlison, a few years ago he purchased an island off the southern coast of Rio de Janeiro, and has the documentation to prove it. Richarlison says Bolsonaro tried to buy it from him, and when he refused a lawyer named Willer Tomaz simply turned up and annexed it. “These guys took the island without spending a penny, as far as I know,” Richarlison claimed in an Instagram video that has been viewed more than 31 million times. Tomaz has accused Richarlison of lying, arguing that he has a public deed registered at the notary’s office. Bolsonaro, for his part, has denied any connection with the island in question and described Richarlison’s intervention as “politically motivated”. Continue reading...

item.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
item.description: Max Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amends Premier League top scorers After seven games, Nottingham Forest’s record is eerily similar to last season: five points, five goals scored. A year ago Forest’s eighth game was a 3-0 home loss to Chelsea that marked the end for Ange Postecoglou , the second of four managers to occupy the dugout last term. There is no suggestion that Oliver Glasner is under similar scrutiny yet, but the Austrian needs to find solutions for the league’s lowest scorers. Morgan Gibbs-White is available after missing the narrow defeat by Arsenal , while Liam Delap may benefit from a return to familiar surroundings – 12 of his 14 career Premier League goals were scored for Ipswich, six of them at Portman Road. “What we need to improve is getting [Delap] into more positions where he can score,” Glasner said before Friday evening’s game. “He’s one of our best finishers.” Gary O’Neil also lacks a standout scorer, but he is squeezing goals out of his side. Eight different Ipswich players have scored in seven games; only Brighton and Brentford can better that total this season. item.title: Bournemouth enjoy night to remember as 10-man Milan fail to weather storm
item.description: This was a momentous night in Bournemouth’s history, although the truth is they would have been given a far sterner examination by Coventry or Hull. Whatever this rotten impersonation of a Milan side was, it bore no relation to those that forged such a celebrated history. The visitors resembled holograms even before their goalkeeper Mike Maignan, with an extraordinary rush of blood resulting in a penalty and red card, rendered their task impossible. They never showed the slightest hint of putting up a fight. Bournemouth simply swamped the seven-time European champions and, amid a swirling south coast storm that rarely let up, could depart singing in the rain. Amine Adli’s sumptuous late free-kick, curled left-footed from 22 yards, meant they could finish the evening with the flourish they deserved. Their joy was clear at full time and met disapproval from some of Milan’s staff, who appeared to take umbrage in a short-lived fracas near the tunnel afterwards. Continue reading...

item.title: Haiti move Nations League home clash with USA to Miami amid gang violence crisis
item.description: Concacaf approves exceptional hosting arrangement Haiti to face US at Nu Stadium on 14 November Miami’s Haitian community offers home advantage Concacaf on Thursday announced it has approved Haiti’s request to relocate their Nations League quarter-final first leg against the United States on 14 November from Kingston, Jamaica, to Miami in an “exceptional hosting arrangement”. Haiti have been unable to play nominal “home” games within their borders since July 2021, with the United Nations estimating that 90% of the capital of Port-au-Prince – including the national stadium – is controlled by violent gangs. Haiti’s match, the first leg of a home-and-away series against the US, had been booked for Kingston. The Grenadiers played their 2026 World Cup qualifiers in Curaçao, Aruba and Barbados. However, the Nations League format slated Curaçao and Jamaica to host their matches on the same night as Haiti’s, shunting Haiti to Sabina Park, the home of the Jamaica national team until their current venue opened in 1962. Now a cricket ground, Sabina Park hosted two of Haiti’s Nations League qualifiers. Continue reading...

item.title: Bruno Guimarães had sleepless nights before Newcastle exit but hopes for same ‘love’ at Arsenal
item.description: Midfielder says there were a lot of tears as he said goodbye at St James’ Park but he is enjoying the remorselessness at his new club For Bruno Guimarães, it was a time to show his steeliness, to fix his eyes on the prize – even if he knew it would surely mean them welling up. And then some. It was a tumultuous summer for the Brazil midfielder. A fine World Cup on a personal level was marred by a crucial penalty miss in the last-16 loss against Norway . Now he had the dream move lined up to Arsenal but it could not happen without breaking some hearts at Newcastle. Guimarães admits he lay awake at night as the emotions swirled. How could he leave Newcastle, the club where he made so many connections and enjoyed so many highs after joining from Lyon in January 2022 ? There were the Champions League qualifications and, above all, the Carabao Cup triumph in 2025 that ended a 70-year wait for a domestic trophy. On the other hand, how could he resist Arsenal and the prospect of competing regularly for the game’s top honours? Continue reading...

item.title: Nottingham Forest’s false start places early focus on Glasner and Delap
item.description: Austrian’s tactics need adapting to but Forest are in the bottom three and their owner is not the patient type Sitting 19th in the Premier League was not the plan for Nottingham Forest after the arrival of a highly acclaimed manager and a £45m striker to fuel their ambitions. The fates of Oliver Glasner and Liam Delap are intertwined and with the stark stats of zero home goals and a solitary point at the City Ground it is not the dream start they were aiming for. As Delap prepares to return to Ipswich, where his career ignited, on Friday night, Forest are remaining calm. There is a desperation to get away from the short-termism that caused so many problems; 12 months ago, they were on their third head coach of a disappointing season. This summer they were ruthless with the removal of Vítor Pereira, who had done a fine job to escape the drop, because they saw an opportunity to upgrade with Glasner, hoping he could transform Forest like he did Crystal Palace. item.title: Manchester City have been a joy to watch but they became detached from their roots | Philipp Lahm
item.description: City behaved much like other top clubs but their rule-breaking deserves to be punished. The Bundesliga, where members have a controlling stake, can show the way forward Do we have to reassess Manchester City now? In my columns, I have repeatedly engaged with this club and its key figures. Looking back at what I have written over the years, I believe it remains beyond question that the team have achieved greatness. I always loved watching them: they were a true unit on the pitch, a finely tuned orchestra. I would also write all over again that the conductor, Pep Guardiola, masters his craft like few others. I could recognise his teams even if they were wearing the wrong shirts and the game was broadcast in black and white – by the passes, the distances between the players and the intelligence of their interplay. It is no wonder Guardiola inspires others to become managers; look at Vincent Kompany, Mikel Arteta, Enzo Maresca, and perhaps some time Ilkay Gündogan and Rodri. Continue reading...

item.title: Too much Overlap? Gary Neville’s podcast empire knows no bounds
item.description: The Overlap has gone daily, with Steven Gerrard and Joe Hart among the latest additions to an ever-growing family Viewed in 2026, Nathan Barley, Chris Morris’s 2005 sitcom, shows remarkable prescience about the last two decades of metropolitan life, from smartphone addiction and digital derangement to sheer existential vapidity. When Barley’s character referred to his occupation as “self-facilitating media node”, Morris and co-writer Charlie Brooker were way ahead on the creator economy. What the pair failed to predict was ex-footballers joining the sector in droves. These days, if you are a former footballer without a podcast or YouTube channel, then did you ever really play the game? Setting aside the Gary Lineker Goalhanger empire, manspreading its centrist-dad agenda into issues way beyond guffaws with Micah Richards and Alan Shearer, there is Gary Neville to rule them all. Manchesterism’s second-most influential practitioner has been on heavy manoeuvres. Unlike Lineker’s productions, the Overlap’s output continues to stick largely to football; a rugby podcast was mothballed in February, though its cricket equivalent continues. Continue reading...

His work here was done, Hansi Flick invited him to take the weight off his feet and his shoulders, not that he wanted to. First, though, he took Lamine Yamal’s head in his hands and, leaning in away from the amateur lip readers, tried to make himself heard over the noise. “I told him I was proud of him because he played a fantastic game,” he said. At least he could think of something. When Lamine Yamal had opened the scoring just nine minutes into the match that was supposed to find out how good Barcelona really were, it hadn’t been easy. Nothing erudite, anyway. On the morning that Barcelona went to Betis – first v third, a proper opponent at last – Jorge Valdano had lamented that sometimes he doesn’t have the words, and he always has the words. Valdano had just watched Lamine do that , whatever that was , in Istanbul – an “almost rabona ”, the kid called it – and now he had a problem. “If he keeps doing strange things, we’re not going to be able to explain it,” he wrote . His work here was done, Hansi Flick invited him to take the weight off his feet and his shoulders, not that he wanted to. First, though, he took Lamine Yamal’s head in his hands and, leaning in away from the amateur lip readers, tried to make himself heard over the noise. “I told him I was proud of him because he played a fantastic game,” he said. At least he could think of something. When Lamine Yamal had opened the scoring just nine minutes into the match that was supposed to find out how good Barcelona really were, it hadn’t been easy. Nothing erudite, anyway. On the morning that Barcelona went to Betis – first v third, a proper opponent at last – Jorge Valdano had lamented that sometimes he doesn’t have the words, and he always has the words. Valdano had just watched Lamine do that , whatever that was , in Istanbul – an “almost rabona ”, the kid called it – and now he had a problem. “If he keeps doing strange things, we’re not going to be able to explain it,” he wrote . item.description: Diego Gómez’s wondergoal in a five-star demolition is just the latest in an impressive run of results for the south coast team Sign up for our free newsletter here For two or three years now, it’s been standard to nod approvingly at how well-run Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth are, and to move on. What else is there to say? It’s true, of course – these are sides who have made the most of relatively limited resources. But there’s also an underlying assumption in the designation: that these are clubs who have no higher aspiration, that their limit is earning praise for upper mid-table finishes. This season, perhaps, offers an opportunity to change that. Other than Arsenal, every major club is undergoing significant transition. Manchester City may have started the season with seven straight wins, but there’s every chance the punishment for their multiple breaches of Premier League regulations takes them out of the race for the top five. In that context, why shouldn’t one of those efficient smaller sides qualify for the Champions League? Continue reading...

item.title: Europe is a blast – but more a curse than a blessing if you are not a Premier League super-club I Jonathan Wilson
item.description: The four Premier League clubs playing in the lesser continental competitions face each other on Sunday – but three are struggling domestically The sun shone. The temperature was in the high 20s. There was a mood of great conviviality. If you were struggling with the official allocation, it turned out you could just email the president of Torreense and he’d sort you out. Were these “Nuno-tickets” real? It turned out they were. Not only that, but you could sit anywhere you wanted in a stadium too big for the game and, if you happened to have gravitated to the comfortable hospitality seating at the back of the lower tier, the beer was inexplicably free. Locals in Leiria seemed bewildered but could hardly have been more accommodating. A beer pump had been installed outside a patisserie on the Praça Francisco Rodrigues Lobo, whose owner soon found fans happy to help stack empty barrels if that facilitated the free flow of Sagres. “There was a meeting at the town hall to explain these are not hooligans,” said the owner of a radical leftist flammkuchen restaurant between the square and the cathedral. “They told us the club comes from the labour movement and I found that very interesting.” And how had she found the fans? “Noisy, but with a quirky sense of humour.” Continue reading...

item.title: James McClean: ‘Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen’
item.description: The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career “The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.” McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. item.content:encoded: The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career “The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.” McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. item.description: Defender may not be blameless in team’s struggles but his criticism goes to the heart of what has gone wrong at the club Heartbreaking: the worst defender you know just made a great point. And no, nobody would describe Lisandro Martínez as the ideal person to scrutinise Manchester United’s indifferent start to the season , given that his high-profile defensive errors against Fulham and Tottenham are partly responsible for it. “We’re all trying to find the guy who did this,” Martínez burbles on Amazon Prime after United’s 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid on Tuesday night, dressed in a hot dog costume and throwing his arms out in mock innocence. For those with no interest in engaging with what Martínez actually had to say, this alone will be sufficient grounds to ignore him. Already you can sense the squeamishness of former players for whom the violation of an omertà is the real cardinal sin here, a phantom limb that still tingles years after they last stepped into a dressing room. “Disrespectful,” reckoned Wayne Rooney. “I don’t feel like he’s got the right,” agreed Ashley Young. “These things don’t end well, man,” Rio Ferdinand observed on his podcast. item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.
